response.translation: Then again there are notes higher and lower than those, and then again others than those, until we arrive at the highest and lowest [216] note of all. But the most admirable Lycus does not perceive that he is abolishing all these things when he says: 'It seems to me impossible and impracticable, for one who considers these matters, that the hot, in the respect in which it is conceived (I mean in respect of the warmth itself), should have any variation relative to another.' A fine thing, if by saying that colour does not differ from colour, insofar as it is colour, he abolishes the art of painting, which sets out a red colour, and white and black and yellow, and all the others of that kind. For his argument is surely far more plausible when stated about colours in the way it has now been stated about the hot: for we say that hot differs from hot, but not that it is in every way its contrary; whereas colour not only differs from colour, but black is in its very nature most contrary to white.

[217] 'And how is it possible,' Lycus might say, 'for something to be contrary to colour in the respect in which it is conceived as being colour?' And he will speak the truth, yes by the gods, so far as colour qua colour is concerned, in holding that one colour does not differ at all from another; but just as this is true, so too is that other point: that white not only differs from black, but differs so much as to be most contrary to it. 'And how is it possible,' perhaps those who champion the views of Lycus will say, 'for it to be at once the same and at once most contrary? And how can white be so to black?' To them we shall answer just this much: that if it is not possible for white to be at once both contrary to and the same as black, let them choose one of the two. For Plato thinks it possible, as indeed do Aristotle and Theophrastus, that one thing, being the same as another in genus, should nevertheless have so great a difference in species as to be most contrary to it. But if these people do not think that both are true, let them choose the more evident account.

renderings.english: so far as colour (qua colour) is concerned

uncertain_greek: ὅσον ἐπὶ χρώματος καὶ τὸ χρῶμα

response.translation: [218] And the more evident is, inasmuch as it is agreed by all men, that white is contrary to black. And indeed, if this is true, and they themselves think that the two accounts cannot both be true, the one asserting that white is contrary to black and the other that it is the same, they will not rightly say that white does not differ at all from black insofar as it is colour. Now the man who in Plato's writing converses with Socrates was perhaps pardonable in preventing Socrates from dividing pleasure from pleasure by a difference. For there was then, I suppose, no book teaching any such thing, namely that it is possible for many things that are the same in genus as many others nevertheless to differ to such a degree as to have a form and nature most contrary to one another. But since the Philebus was written by Plato teaching the truth, if Lycus did not read the book at all, I admire Lycus for his education; if, having read it, he did not understand it, I marvel at his intelligence; and if, having understood it, he was not persuaded, I congratulate him on his judgement.

O, by Zeus, does someone put an argument by questioning who has not learned even the [219] first elements of dialectic? Is there any Greek man, physician or grammarian or rhetor or philosopher or in general anyone else whatever who lays claim to learning, who has not read Plato's Philebus? And yet why do I say the Philebus? For it is not in this alone that Plato taught the argument before us; he also recalled it in many other books, of which the most admirable Lycus ought to have read at least a single one, laying claim as he does to scientific arguments. For it is shameful for one who undertakes to refute Hippocrates and who puts arguments that are conclusive, as he thinks, to appear not to have learned even the first things of what is taught in the schools of the philosophers. But, by Zeus, his example about liquids is wonderful. For he means this too: that they do not differ from one another at all, if all are liquids, while in the respect in which some are sour, others acerbic, others salty, others sweet, in that respect they differ; and in this he does not listen to himself.

For by saying in what respect liquids differ, he thinks he establishes that there is no difference in them, but that Hippocrates spoke of a difference in vain, and that Theophrastus wrote in vain [220] a whole treatise on flavour. And yet this very name, 'flavour' (chylos), indicates a certain difference of liquid; but nevertheless, although it is a difference of liquid, it is by nature divided again into other differences. It is no wonder, however, that Lycus, having come to such a degree of lack of education as to think that there is an astringent quality in vinegar, should dare to write such a rebuttal against Hippocrates. For things so evident were known even to Dioscorides of Anazarbus, and to all the others who wrote treatises on materia medica. At any rate in these they name some things briny, others salty, others bitter, others sweet, others austere, others acerbic, others astringent, others pungent, others sour. But the most admirable Lycus either does not know at all that the sour quality differs from the astringent, or he has his sense of taste maimed, since he does not perceive at all the differences among flavours.

It seems, then, that he perceives vinegar as he does pear and medlar and apple and quince, although all men call some apples [221] sour, some astringent, and others sweet, just as, I think, they call pomegranates too sour and astringent and sweet. In wines, at any rate, in which excellence is distinguished from defect, astringency is distinguished from sourness: for the astringent wines are noble, whereas none is sour by nature, but if even a little of such a quality comes upon them, we at once suspect their change into vinegar. Perhaps, then, Lycus did not distinguish sorrel (oxylapathon) or oxalis (oxyalis) from dock and lettuce either, though in them there is not the least share of astringent quality, while both partake abundantly of the sour. It would be a wonder, then, if these have been named from the sour quality while vinegar itself does not partake of it. But Lycus, who does not preserve even the common senses, dares to accuse Hippocrates. So again he has taken cognisance of the inquiry among the natural philosophers concerning the number of flavours! For on this view, it seems, flavour does not differ from flavour at all, insofar as it is flavour.

I would gladly hear, then, of which existing things such differences are: sweet, sour, pungent, [222] bitter, salty, briny, acerbic, austere, astringent, oily. For unless they are perhaps of flavours, they are of sounds or colours or odours, or else they come to cognition through touch. For besides these we have no other sense. But they are five in all: taste and hearing and sight and smell and touch. And just as we discern different sensibles by the different senses, so by taste we discern flavours. And as in liquids the differences are many, in the same way also in the senses. And yet insofar as they are senses, they do not differ; but the most dialectical Lycus will not allow us to say that the differences mentioned are in flavours, nor in the senses, which all men know, nor in colours: white and black and grey and yellow and tawny, red and crimson and dark blue. For neither does colour differ from colour insofar as it is colour. All physicians and philosophers, then, are mad, who believe that the differences mentioned are differences of colours,
uncertain_greek: εἰ μὴ γὰρ χυμῶν ἴσως ἤτοι

response.translation: and that the sour and bitter and pungent, and all the others I mentioned a little earlier, are differences of flavours, [223] as also of the senses themselves. For neither does colour differ from colour, insofar as it is colour, just as neither does sense from sense nor flavour from flavour, just as neither does fever from fever, since neither does hot from hot. Mad, then, are the physicians who have written of many differences of fevers: the kausos, the leipyria, the epialos, the typhōdēs, the pestilential, and the semitertian, quotidian, tertian and quartan. But Lycus himself elsewhere writes of differences of fevers, as indeed of almost all other things. What, then, came over him that he has now forgotten to divide each of the other things into its proper differences, he who, concerning the fire kindled from chaff, which goldworkers are accustomed to use, thinks there is no difference except in relation to the other materials?
uncertain_greek: ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸ τὰς ἄλλας ὕλας

response.translation: For neither does fire differ from fire, insofar as it is fire, except by the more and the less [224] (for it is possible for fire to be strong and weak); and thinking that the fire of chaff is the weakest, he says it is reserved for the working of gold. For the gold melts away and runs off when it comes near a stronger flame. But, my excellent Lycus, someone might say to him, I think, if you had listened to the natural philosophers inquiring how flames are generated, you would, I think, have perceived the differences in them. I, then, condensing as far as possible into the briefest compass an account of no small length, will explain to you about them. You see, I think, that from the burning material an exhalation arises in parts drawn apart from one another, and some air, enclosed between them, is of necessity, surely, heated. And it admits of a very great difference in the more and the less.

But also the intervals between the bodies carried upward are not equal in all flames, just as neither is the nature of the exhalation itself; rather, the parts of the burning material that rush upward have differed from [225] one another in largeness and smallness, and in density and rarity, and in that some are half-burnt, others as it were wholly burnt, or in general that some are more, others less, converted into fire. When, then, these appear to have so great a difference, and the air that has received them is at one time more thoroughly heated by them, at another less, it is necessary that a very great variety arise, and no small difference of the flame. For the unlikeness of the mixture produces the multitude of differences. And just as what concerns fire has been stated ignorantly by Lycus, in the same way, I think, also when, saying that 'much hot' is conceived in three ways, he goes through each of the meanings. For he says that 'much hot' is conceived in one sense according to substance, in another according to the intensity of the quality, and in another according to the strength of its proper activity.
